explain.say: A big container ship can carry over 20,000 steel boxes, all in standard sizes, so cranes, lorries and trains anywhere can handle them. Loading starts when a lorry or train brings each box to the quay.

explain.say: Below deck, steel cell guides steer each box into its slot; on deck, boxes are locked together and lashed with rods. A computer plans every position so heavy boxes go low, the ship stays balanced, and boxes for the first port come off first.

faq.q: Why are shipping containers all the same size?
faq.a: Standard sizes, mostly 20 and 40 feet long, mean any crane, ship, lorry or train can handle any container. Ships are measured in TEU, twenty-foot equivalent units.
The spreader is the frame hanging from the crane that grabs a container. It has twistlocks at each corner that lock into holes in the container's corner fittings.
asks: How does a crane grab a container?

faq.q: How fast can a container crane work?
faq.a: A ship-to-shore crane typically moves around 25 to 40 containers an hour, and several cranes work on one big ship at the same time.
asks: How long does it take to load a container ship?

faq.q: What holds containers in place on a ship?
faq.a: Below deck, vertical steel guides called cell guides hold the stacks. On deck, twistlocks join boxes together and steel lashing rods tie them down.
asks: Why don't containers fall off ships?

faq.q: How is a container ship loaded in the right order?
faq.a: Planners use computers to give every box a slot. Heavy boxes go low for stability, weight is balanced side to side, and boxes for the first port go where they can be reached first.
asks: Who decides where containers go on a ship?

facts: American businessman Malcom McLean pioneered container shipping in 1956.
Container ship sizes are measured in TEU, twenty-foot equivalent units.
The largest container ships can carry more than 20,000 TEU.
